newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - RETAIL SALES, PPI KEY.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - RETAIL SALES, PPI KEY.

text.p: Trying to predict what might happen in the U.S. Treasury market on Wednesday has proven to be a lesson in futility.
With a double-dose of key economic data due, players said the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond will either rise to 6.75 percent or fall to 6.50 percent.

"The market has moved up and down the past few days on no news, so when we get news, the market will have a tremendous move," said a trader at a large U.S. bank/dealer. "We can easily (rise or fall) 15 basis points on news."

Treasuries fell sharply off their highs on Tuesday. The 30-year ended down 1/4-after having been 3/4 point higher in mid-afternoon trading. Its yield continued to rise, closing at an ominous 6.66 percent.
"The market trades long," said a trader. "It feels lousy going out the door" ahead of Wednesday's data, which include retail sales and the Producer Price Index (PPI) for July at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
In recent months, market participants have said retail sales is the most important economic indicator.
"To dismiss PPI out of hand would be a mistake," said Pat Alexander, head trader at BancAmerica Securities. "But retail sales is clearly what the market is more focused on."

Economists surveyed by Reuters expected retail sales data to show a rise of 0.7 percent in July after rising 0.5 percent in June. Sales excluding autos were seen up 0.5 percent in July after a 0.3 percent rise in June.
"If we get downward revisions to prior months, that will add fuel to the fire," Alexander said.
He said PPI would also garner a lot of attention, especially since the index has fallen six straight months.
Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Securities, concurred, noting that the market will react to the combination of both sets of data.
Both the overall and core PPI were expected to have risen 0.1 percent in July. The market, however, fears the overall figure may be up as much as 0.3 percent.

"If we get strong retail sales -- both total and nonauto -- and a pickup in inflation, I think the bond is going up to 6.75 percent," Flanagan said. "If they are both weak, we will head back to 6.50 percent."
The likelhood of both sets of data pointing in the same direction is rather slim.
"Most likely, we will be in between," said one trader, adding that the data should be a mixed bag. "But it is going to be choppy trading."
Players figure that the market has more room to fall than rise, since the notion of a "Brave New World" has yet to gain universal acceptance.
After rising to year-and -a half highs through July, "the first sign of trouble, people bailed," Flanagan said.
